name: SBI PO
tagline: India's most sought-after bank officer exam: Probationary Officer at the country's largest bank

overview.about: SBI recruits Probationary Officers (Junior Management Grade Scale-I) through a three-phase process: Prelims, Mains (objective + descriptive) and Phase III (psychometric test, group exercise and interview). Final merit combines Mains and Phase III, normalised to 75 : 25.
eligibility: Graduation in any discipline from a recognised university (final-year/semester students may apply provisionally, subject to proof by the date in the notification)
Age 21–30 years (e.g. as on 01.04.2026 for the 2025-26 cycle); relaxation: SC/ST 5 yrs, OBC-NCL 3 yrs, PwBD 10 yrs
Limited number of attempts for General/EWS candidates as specified in the notification
Indian citizen (or other categories defined in the notification)

pattern.note: Separate timing per section; overall cut-off only (no sectional cut-off)

pattern.paper: Phase II Mains — Reasoning & Computer Aptitude
pattern.note: −0.25 of the question's marks per wrong answer

pattern.paper: Phase II Mains — Data Analysis & Interpretation

pattern.note: Current affairs of the last ~6 months
Email/letter, essay, situation analysis or précis; typed on computer; evaluated only if objective cut-offs are cleared

pattern.paper: Phase III — Psychometric test, Group Exercise & Interview
pattern.note: Group Exercise 20 + Interview 30; psychometric test is qualifying

topics.t: Number system — divisibility, HCF & LCM, remainders, unit digits
Number series — missing number, wrong number, new-pattern (all types)
Data interpretation — table, bar, line, pie, radar & mixed charts
Caselet DI, missing DI & arithmetic DI
Logical reasoning — course of action, cause & effect, inferences, strengthen/weaken
MS Office — Word, Excel, PowerPoint & shortcuts
Vocabulary — synonyms, antonyms, idioms & phrasal verbs
Banking history, structure & types of banks
Regulators & financial institutions (SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM, NHB, NPCI, DICGC)
Financial markets — money, capital, bond & forex
Banking products, terms & the Negotiable Instruments Act
Government schemes (credit, farm, health, housing, savings)
Union Budget, fiscal terms & Economic Survey basics
Current affairs & static GK — sources and method

cards.title: How selection works
cards.body: Prelims is **qualifying only**: roughly 10× the vacancies are called for Mains. Mains (objective 200 + descriptive 30 = **230**) and Phase III (**50**) form the final merit, normalised to **75 : 25**. So Mains decides most of your rank.

cards.title: Final score formula
points: Mains part = (Mains marks ÷ 230) × 75
Phase III part = (GE + Interview ÷ 50) × 25
Final (out of 100) = Mains part + Phase III part

cards.title: Prelims: overall cut-off only
cards.body: SBI PO Prelims has **no sectional cut-off**. Maximise your strongest section, but don't ignore any: 20 minutes is fixed for each, and unused time is lost. Target about 70% accuracy-weighted attempts in each section.

cards.title: Mains: sectional cut-offs apply
cards.body: Mains has sectional cut-offs. GA (60 marks for 60 Q) has the **best marks per minute**, so consistent current-affairs revision from 6 months before the exam pays off most. English carries just 20 marks for 40 Q: attempt fast, don't over-invest.

cards.title: Negative marking maths
cards.body: Each wrong answer costs ¼ of that question's marks. If you can eliminate **two of five** options, a guess has a positive expected score (1/3 × 1 − 2/3 × 0.25 = +0.17). Blind guesses on five options give 0.

cards.q: A candidate scores 138/230 in Mains and 35/50 in Phase III. Final score out of 100?
Which statement about SBI PO Prelims is correct?
options: Each section has a sectional cut-off
Prelims marks count in the final merit
cards.explain: SBI PO Prelims has only an overall cut-off; it is qualifying and its marks are not added to the final merit.

cards.q: If you can eliminate two of five options, guessing among the rest gives an expected score per question of about:

notes.p:
SBI PO has three phases. **Prelims** (objective, 1 hour) is only a filter: its marks are **not added** to the final merit. Roughly ten times the number of vacancies are called to **Mains**. Mains has an **objective test of 200 marks** and a **descriptive test of 30 marks** (total **230**). **Phase III** has a psychometric test (qualifying), a **Group Exercise (20)** and an **Interview (30)**, together **50 marks**.

The final merit list combines Mains and Phase III after converting them to **75 : 25**. Because Mains carries three-quarters of the weight, your real rank is built in Mains.
points: Prelims: qualifying, overall cut-off only.
Mains: sectional and overall cut-offs; 230 marks.
Phase III: 50 marks; psychometric test is qualifying.
Final score out of 100 = Mains (75) + Phase III (25).
Section-wise question counts and timings are revised from time to time; check the latest notification.

notes.h: Worked example: calculating your final score
notes.p:
Formula: **Final = (Mains ÷ 230) × 75 + (Phase III ÷ 50) × 25**.

**Example 1:** Mains 115/230, Phase III 30/50.
Mains part = 115 ÷ 230 × 75 = 0.5 × 75 = **37.5**.
Phase III part = 30 ÷ 50 × 25 = 0.6 × 25 = **15**.
Final = 37.5 + 15 = **52.5/100**.

**Example 2: what is a Mains mark worth?** One Mains mark = 75 ÷ 230 ≈ **0.33** final marks. One Phase III mark = 25 ÷ 50 = **0.5** final marks. So a single interview mark is worth more than a Mains mark, but Mains has 230 marks to play with, so it still decides most ranks. Gaining 15 extra Mains marks (≈ 4.9 final marks) is often easier than gaining 10 extra Phase III marks (5 final marks).

SBI PO Prelims has **no sectional cut-off**, but each section has a **fixed 20-minute timer**, so you cannot carry time across sections. Aim for steady, accurate attempts in all three sections rather than gambling on one.
points: **English:** RC and error-based questions first, then para jumbles; avoid over-reading options.
**Quant:** simplification/approximation and series first, then quadratic, arithmetic and one DI set.
**Reasoning:** inequality, syllogism, coding and direction first; then one or two easier puzzles.
Keep accuracy above about **85–90%** on attempted questions; with negative marking, careless attempts cost a lot.

notes.p:
Each wrong answer costs **¼ of the marks** for that question.

**Worked example:** a 1-mark question with five options.
Blind guess: expected score = (1/5)(1) − (4/5)(0.25) = 0.2 − 0.2 = **0**.
After eliminating two options (three left): (1/3)(1) − (2/3)(0.25) = 0.333 − 0.167 ≈ **+0.17**.
After eliminating three (two left): (1/2)(1) − (1/2)(0.25) = 0.5 − 0.125 = **+0.375**.
Rule: **guess only after eliminating at least two options**. Blind guessing adds risk without adding expected marks.

Mains has sectional cut-offs and sectional timers. The **General/Economy/Banking Awareness** section gives the best marks per minute because questions are factual and quick, so six months of steady current-affairs revision pays off the most. Reasoning and Data Analysis are where scores differ most between candidates; practise high-level puzzles and mixed DI daily. English carries relatively fewer marks: attempt it fast and accurately.

The **descriptive test** (30 marks) is evaluated with the objective paper in mind, so do not neglect typing practice.
Avoid these.
points: Studying only for Prelims and starting Mains preparation late.
Ignoring GA until the last month.
Changing the section order on exam day without having tried it in mocks.
Blind guessing at the end of a section.
Neglecting Phase III preparation; it is 25% of the final score.

notes.p: Key points.
points: Prelims: qualifying, overall cut-off, 20 minutes per section.
Mains: 200 objective + 30 descriptive = 230.
Phase III: GE 20 + Interview 30 = 50; psychometric qualifying.
Final = (Mains/230) × 75 + (Phase III/50) × 25.
Guess only after eliminating two options.
GA has the best marks per minute in Mains.

cards.title: What is asked
cards.body: 30 marks in 30 minutes, typed on screen. Recent papers ask **two** tasks from: formal **email/letter**, **essay**, **précis/report writing** and **situation analysis**. Content, structure, grammar and staying within the word limit all count.

cards.title: Formal email skeleton
points: To / Subject: one clear line
Salutation: Dear Sir/Madam,
Para 1: purpose; Para 2: details/facts; Para 3: request or action
Closing: Yours sincerely / Regards, name, designation

cards.title: Essay structure (≈250 words)
points: Intro (2–3 lines): define the topic, add one fact
Body (2 paras): benefits/causes and challenges
Way forward: 2–3 concrete steps (government, RBI, banks, citizens)
Conclusion: one balanced line

cards.title: Situation analysis
cards.body: You are put in a workplace dilemma (e.g. a customer complains loudly, a colleague bends a rule). Show **empathy, rule-compliance and escalation**: understand the issue, follow bank policy, communicate clearly, involve the manager when needed, and record the action.

cards.title: Précis rules
cards.body: Write about **one-third** of the original length, in your own words, in the **third person and past tense** where relevant. No examples, no new opinions. Give it a short title.

cards.title: Practise typing
cards.body: The test is typed, so practise writing 250 words in **15 minutes** on a keyboard. Keep a bank of topics: digital payments, financial inclusion, cyber fraud, green finance, AI in banking, MSME credit.

cards.q: An original passage has 300 words. A précis should be roughly:
cards.explain: A précis is about one-third of the original length: 300/3 = 100 words.

cards.q: In a situation-analysis answer, which response is best?
options: Ignore the issue to avoid conflict
Bend the rules to satisfy the customer
Listen, follow bank policy and escalate when needed
Ask the customer to visit another branch
cards.explain: Examiners reward empathy, compliance with policy and proper escalation.

notes.h: What the descriptive test looks like
notes.p:
The SBI PO descriptive test is **30 marks in 30 minutes**, **typed on screen** right after the objective Mains paper. Recent papers ask **two tasks** chosen from a formal **email or letter**, an **essay**, a **précis or report**, and a **situation analysis**. Examiners mark **content, structure, grammar and adherence to the word limit**.

Because time is tight, you need ready templates and fast typing. Aim to type 250 words in about 15 minutes with few errors.
points: Plan for 2 minutes, write for 11–12 minutes, review for 1–2 minutes per task.
Stay within the word limit: exceeding it or falling far short can cost marks.
Use short paragraphs; on screen they are easier to read.

notes.p: Keep a fixed structure so you only think about content.
points: **To / Subject:** one clear line (e.g. 'Subject: Request to enable SMS alerts on savings account').
**Salutation:** Dear Sir/Madam,
**Paragraph 1:** who you are and the purpose.
**Paragraph 2:** the facts or details (dates, account type, issue).
**Paragraph 3:** the specific request or action expected.
**Closing:** Yours sincerely / Regards, name, designation or contact details.
Tone: polite, direct, no slang or emojis.

notes.h: Essay structure with a worked outline
notes.p:
A 250-word essay needs **four parts**: introduction, two body paragraphs, way forward and conclusion.

**Worked outline: 'Cyber fraud in digital banking'** (about 250 words)
**Intro (40 words):** digital payments have grown rapidly with UPI; fraud attempts have grown alongside.
**Body 1 – causes (60 words):** phishing and fake KYC messages, SIM swap, low awareness among new users, use of remote-access apps.
**Body 2 – impact (50 words):** financial loss, loss of trust in digital channels, burden on banks and police.
**Way forward (70 words):** customer awareness campaigns; banks' real-time fraud monitoring; quick reporting via the 1930 helpline and cybercrime.gov.in; stronger device and SIM verification.
**Conclusion (30 words):** safe digital banking needs vigilant customers and alert banks.
Total ≈ 40 + 60 + 50 + 70 + 30 = **250 words**.

**Précis:** write about **one-third** of the original length (300 words → about 100), in your own words, usually in the third person. Keep only main ideas; drop examples and repetition; give it a short title.

**Situation analysis:** you are placed in a workplace dilemma. Examiners reward answers that show **empathy, rule-compliance, clear communication and escalation**.
points: Step 1: state the problem in one line.
Step 2: list the options and their consequences.
Step 3: choose the option that follows bank policy and treats the customer fairly.
Step 4: say how you will communicate, involve the manager if needed, and record the action.
Never suggest breaking rules to please a customer or ignoring a complaint.

notes.p: These lose easy marks.
points: No subject line in an email.
One long paragraph instead of structured parts.
Copying sentences into a précis instead of rewriting.
Adding opinions or examples in a précis.
Spending 20 minutes on the first task and rushing the second.

notes.p: Before the exam:
points: 30 marks, 30 minutes, typed, two tasks.
Email: subject → salutation → purpose → details → request → close.
Essay: intro, two body paragraphs, way forward, conclusion.
Précis = one-third length, own words, title.
Situation: empathy + policy + escalation + record.
Practise typing 250 words in 15 minutes.

chapters.title: Phase III: psychometric test, GE & interview

cards.title: Three parts
cards.body: **Psychometric test**: personality/behaviour assessment, qualifying. **Group Exercise** (20 marks): discussion or task with other candidates. **Interview** (30 marks): panel of senior officers. Phase III makes up **25%** of the final score.

cards.title: Group Exercise
cards.body: Speak early but not first if unsure; add **facts and structure** ('Let's look at three angles…'); invite quieter members; summarise at the end if the group lets you. Interrupting and aggression lose marks.

cards.title: Interview topics
cards.body: Expect: why banking/why SBI, your degree and hometown, SBI's products and recent initiatives, current repo rate and MPC stance, a recent budget/economy topic, and situational questions. Answers of 30–60 seconds work best.

cards.title: Psychometric test
cards.body: There are no right answers, but **inconsistency** across similar statements is flagged. Answer honestly and consistently; don't try to guess what the 'ideal banker' would say on every item.

cards.q: How many marks do the Group Exercise and Interview together carry in SBI PO Phase III?
The psychometric test in SBI PO Phase III is:
cards.explain: It is a qualifying assessment; merit comes from GE and interview.

notes.p: Phase III has three parts: a **psychometric test** (personality/behaviour assessment, **qualifying**), a **Group Exercise (20 marks)** and an **Interview (30 marks)**. GE and interview together carry **50 marks**, which make up **25%** of the final score. The panel is looking for a person who can lead a branch team, handle customers and adapt to postings anywhere in India.

There are no 'right' answers in a psychometric test. It looks at traits such as integrity, teamwork, stress tolerance and customer orientation. The same idea is often asked in **different words**, and contradictions are flagged.
points: Answer honestly and quickly; your first instinct is usually the most consistent.
Do not pick extreme options on every item to look 'perfect'.
Expect statements like 'I prefer working alone' and later 'I enjoy team projects'; your answers should fit together.
Sleep well; fatigue makes answers inconsistent.

notes.p: The GE may be a discussion on a topic or a task the group must complete together. Assessors watch **content, communication, teamwork and leadership**, not who speaks most.
points: Speak early, but if unsure of the topic, listen for 30 seconds first.
Add **structure**: 'Let us look at three angles: customers, banks and the regulator.'
Bring **facts**: one data point or scheme name makes your point stronger.
Invite quieter members ('We haven't heard from you yet') — this shows leadership.
Summarise at the end if the group allows.
Never interrupt aggressively or argue personally.

notes.p: Interview answers of **30–60 seconds** work best. Prepare a short, honest introduction and examples from your own life.
points: **About you:** introduction, graduation subject, hometown economy, hobbies listed in your form.
**Why banking / why SBI:** link to stability, public service, career growth, SBI's reach.
**SBI knowledge:** major products (YONO, home loans, savings schemes), recent initiatives.
**Economy:** current repo rate and MPC stance (check the latest RBI announcement), recent Budget highlights, inflation and growth trends.
**Situational:** handling an angry customer, a colleague bending rules, a rural posting.

notes.h: Worked example: answering a situational question
notes.p:
**Question:** "A senior customer is shouting because his pension has not been credited. What will you do?"
**Model answer in four steps:**
1. **Calm and listen:** offer a seat and listen without interrupting.
2. **Check facts:** look up the account and the pension credit status.
3. **Act within rules:** if the delay is from the pension-paying office, explain and help him raise the request; if it is a bank error, escalate to the branch manager immediately.
4. **Follow up and record:** give a timeline, note the complaint, and call him back.
This answer shows empathy, policy knowledge and ownership — exactly what panels look for.
Avoid these in Phase III.
points: Memorised, long answers that sound rehearsed.
Bluffing when you do not know; say so politely and offer what you do know.
Not knowing details you wrote in your own application.
Dominating the GE or staying silent throughout.
Quoting outdated policy rates.

notes.p: Remember:
points: Psychometric: qualifying; be honest and consistent.
GE 20 + Interview 30 = 50 marks = 25% of final.
GE: structure, facts, inclusion, summary.
Interview: 30–60 second answers.
Situational answers: listen → check → act within rules → follow up.
Know SBI products and latest RBI policy stance.
